Title: Errata killed the Big Vampire Star

Messages.Author: just...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
What happened to all the big vamps? Weenie decks seem to be all the
rave,
even though big vamps are much more fun to play with. The answer lies
in the
fact that quite a lot of rulings from [RTR 19980707] and [RTR 19980623]
were
detrimental to big vampires while the younger vampires were relatively
unaffected. Here's a short list of some of the changes that really hurt
the
big guys. Followed by the one change IMHO that was good for them.

Bad
Return to Innocence
Mind Rape
Golconda (no more Soul Gem deck)
Mask of 1,000 Faces + Atonement (a cool trick that allowed big vamps to
block almost anything and still stay untapped.)
Rotschreck (hurts much more if used against a big vamp. No easy defense)
Rutor's hand - no multiples
Tomb of Rameses

Good
2nd Tradition (now essential for Princes and Justicars)

Now it's important to mention that Weenie vote decks were severely
limited
by the vote-pushing restriction. However, this affected quite a lot of
vote
decks other than Weenie decks, restricting voting to mainly Presence
vote
decks. Also, other types of Weenie decks weren't adversely affected by
the
vote-pushing restriction at all, and may have even been helped by
removing
the vote decks that could have damaged them across table.

Does anyone else think that big vampires need some more help, or has
everyone been swept away in ecstacy by Weenie Tap and Bleed Mania?

Justicar.

Noal is Noal MacDonald, and the reason he doesn't post here anymore is
that he and his group just got so disgusted with the 7/7 errata that they
formed their own setup, the Michigan Jyhad League. You see, it is a tiny
bit selectively-memorious of my dear friend the Atomweaver to say that
almost everyone on the NG agreed with the errata. Noal, Sorrow, myself
and numerous others were, and to some extent still are, VIOLENTLY opposed
to the principle of errata, and actually in some cases to the specific
errata themselves. But now i am the only member of the Complacently Slow-
Minded Minions of Chaos and Entropy who still joins in these debates - i
promised one of our aussie brethren to keep an eye on them and, as he put
it in his charming colonial way, "to keep the bastards honest".

swung too much towards weenies, which was entirely predictable, and WAS
predicted. You spelt out the reasons for this change perfectly cogently
in the first post, and i see no need to add to them. However, Rotshreck
was NOT errata'd, it was just interpreted correctly - previously it had
suffered from a ruling imposed by a functional illiterate [in the
EXTREMELY relative frame of Jyhad text-complexity]. A hearty thank-you to
LSJ for this, from all the aficionados of malkavian out-of-turn rush-
combat.

i don't, however, think that more errata is the answer [except maybe to
clean up some of the Setite cards, and make it possible to play Elder
Intervention AND Pack Tactics]. As i kept saying in the original debates,
if someone is beating up your decks with [to you] boring strategies, then
it is time to change your decks, not to whine about how the rules need
changing so that your own beloved strategy will work. The big guys aren't
dead or useless - you just need new ways to bring them out quickly, and
to make their presence HURT once they are out. i can't remember if the
Goodnight, Sweet Prince deck has been archived [help, Xian?] but that is
one way to do it [the basic idea is CERTAINLY on the net]. Same goes for
the so-called crap clans - check out Matthew Green's excellent Assamite
vote deck.

Curiously enough as i was thinking about data with which to back up some
of my assertions in this post i remembered that the UK gencon final was
AMAZINGLY well-balanced in terms of different kinds of decks. i expect
James C will do his usual excellent tournament report on this so i won't
steal his thunder except by saying that three decks got VPs there -
weenie vote, weenie combat, and Big Cammie Mothersuckers. The less-
successful decks were weenie stealth-bleed and Biggish bleed, and thereby
hangs an interesting tale or two which James will tell once he has got
his moving-to-Cambridge and Shagging-all-the-Nubile-Young-Freshers phase
out of the way.

Jennifer in hopes of a biggish Ravnos with necromancy, and a !Gangrel
girly with necromancy and animalism.

But this is a game mechanic issue, not a "storyline/theme/roleplaying"

>Sunlight. You say that should not burn him either, even is he's at
>zero.

A zero blood vampire is not hurt, just hungry. He won't be going to
torpor on his own unless he takes some damage. Agg damage is defined
in the game mechanics as "damage which cannot be healed by burning
blood". Both of these are stock interpretations, right? If he takes
one point of normal damage (Burst of LeadPipeToTheHead), he can't burn
any blood to heal it and so will bung off to torpor, wounded. If he
takes one point of agg damage (aiee! the bright light), he can't burn
any blood to heal IT, either, and so bungs off to torpor, wounded.
The only difference is that if he had blood, he still wouldn't be able
to burn blood to heal it.

>Just don't ring true to me.

If you -need- an RPG issue, imagine a flash of sunlight through a
window (Burst of Sunlight) from drapes rapidly pulled aside. A
vampire standing in front of that would immediately lunge aside, and
is probably scorched, blackened, and seared all over, looking much
like an overcooked hot dog. He will be headed to torpor for awhile,
since his system obviously can't deal with the shock. So, a superior
Burst of Sunlight is either a larger window, being pushed out a back
door into daylight, etc. etc... which since he has nowhere to
immediately duck out of the way from, does more damage to him,
possibly resulting in him turning into ashes. If he had blood on him,
he could use up his lifeforce/resources to last just long enough to
get back into the comforting shadows, but would still be headed for
torpor from the shock.

the fact that *some* big vampires were hurt. That didn't make big
vampires less attractive to play - it made those big vampires less
attractive to play, it didn't make others less attractive - their
attractiveness, or not, was based on other conditions.

Return to Innocence hit big vampires, yes, but it only hit *some* big
vampires. How often did you ever see, say, Cassandra, Magus Prime, pull
off a Return to Innocence? Did you know people who suddenly found that
Masika suddenly became *the* vampire to include in a deck, just so they
could pull off RtoI? Alexandra? Hitting RtoI wouldn't alter those
vampires, because those vampires barely benefitted from RtoI, in that
they found it shaky, expensive and difficult to pull off - especially if
you've invested in a big vampire, and so don't have many vampires to do
the "I'll wait till you're all tapped out and do it then" routine.

Mind Rape - Again, this doesn't hit big vampires, it hits vampires with
dominate, and predominantly, big vampires with Dominate. Did changing
Mind Rape make Francois Villon less attractive to play, given that he
couldn't play it already? Did it make your "Wynn-Wynn" deck less
viable, given Wynn's sudden inability to abuse Mind Rape, a card he
couldn't use before without significant investment in Master
disciplines? Did Yong Sun suddenly lose all his potency in the same
manner?

Golconda - To say that there could be no more Soul Gem decks is patently
untrue. That there could be no more Soul Gem decks which exploited
Golconda in that manner is true, but look at the deck Chris Berger built
using Aurora to good effect, in an "infinite loop" Soul Gem deck. Soul
Gem was never just for big vampires using Golconda. Also, Golconda
provided, and still provides, a way for you to give someone enough rope
to hang themselves. They either have to lose a vampire and gain pool,
or be "bled" for 2. Under most circumstances, a Methuselah doesn't want
to do *either* of these and, if they pick the worse of the two, they're
even more screwed.

Mask of 1000 Faces + Atonement - Again, you say this acted to the
detriment of big vampires. No, big vampires with obfuscate.

Rotschreck - It could be used against a big vampire before, especially
the aggravated hand damage bunch, and the Gangrel "Wynn-Wynn" deck in
particular. Now, they have to act, come to you, let you block them
(most likely) and then you deal them aggravated damage. A quite
difficult sequence of events, I would have thought.

Tomb of Rameses - Look at the *current* errata. It's very, very viable.
*Very* viable. If you don't think so, that's your problem. It can
still bring out big vampires quickly, it just can't be used as a blood
machine in the process.

Rutor's Hand - And? Was Rutor's Hand only used by big vampires? No, it
wasn't. And even if it was, you single out vampires with Thaumaturgy.

Of the three cards you cite with disciplines, you've just knocked out
vampires with Obfuscate, Thaumaturgy and *superior* Dominate. There are
big vampires out there who want give a monkey's about that. They were
either empowered or not empowered based on other criterion. And the
changes hit smaller vampires, too. The Mask thing stopped weenie
obfuscate vampires doing interesting with Rutor's Hand themselves,
borrowing it from a bigger vampire. And those vampires who the changes
could have conceivably "hit" by having those disciplines couldn't
necessarily use those tricks anyway. An Atoned vampire that couldn't
defend itself in combat, or defend the Atonement from burning, was
useless, and not all vampires with Obfuscate can defend themselves in
combat properly against a concerted attack (and watch out for Immortal
Grapple, of course), so why bother? Similarly, Mind Rape is only
effective if you can get it through - and not everyone with superior
Dominate is empowered with stealth (e.g. Spiridonas, Wilhelm Waldberg,
Lazarus) or, if they themselves are, you have to build a deck dedicated
to that one vampire, because it's quite out of clan (e.g. Marty
Lechtansi, because DOM in a Nos is unusual, Etrius with OBF and pro
which are not too often found in Tremere).

Big vampires were not empowered before the 7/7. *SOME* big vampires
happened to be. Not all, by any means. 7/7 only took the power away
from *those* big vampires, not all big vampires.

assess the table while pushing - who threw vote cards down against me?

single non-damage vote out of my hand on the second one, since I now

transfer out two new weenies and redraw my hand.

Rushing my weenies, in which case I am dead no matter how well my hand
goes. I examine my hand. If I have no damage votes, I make two new
Princes and empty my hand in the process whether I need to or not,
making 8 table votes and a great chance to have a handful of damage
next turn. I probably am in good shape with the four weenies, but I
get a new one from my crypt anyway just in case one gets cancelled or
someone starts discovering a lot of intercept. I get a new vamp every
other turn that way, and if I'm smart, I've stuck 5 Info Highways in
my library so's I get a new vamp -every- turn. If I -do- have damage
votes (probably 3), I don't use them immediately, I toss at least one

not *need* to push vote cards, as I have 5 votes in favor
automatically and probably only 2-3 table votes against me. Again,
assess the table - do I see titled guys likely to come out, or do I
think they can overcome 7 votes easily? If not, I call 3 damage
votes, causing minimum 9 pool loss to my prey -on turn three-. On my
third vote, I empty my hand of all non-damage votes, giving myself
great odds to draw up more. I probably oust my prey next turn if I
draw up 3 more damage votes, although Domain Challenge would be
annoying to have in-hand this early in the game.

Sorrow wrote:
>>I'm not sure where you are going with the above. Out of all the combat
decks, the only way to ensure this, *reliably*, is by using Potence and
Decapitate or using Amaranth and risk the blood hunt. You say that
agg damage PF is a no-no because it too reliably burned vamps, but
then you go on to say that a rush deck needs to be able to reliably get
rid of the opponents vamps. If I missed something, please tell me.>>

Ok. Here is the problem with PF doing aggro damage--Pulled Fangs is a zero
discipline card with no blood cost, very limited play requirements, and
effectively no cost. As such, having it do aggro damage is inordinately
powerful. When the card was designed (under the Jyhad aggro rules), it wasn't
such a bad thing, as it was completely incapable of burning vampires, as one
point of aggro damage from a given source could never burn a vampire. If you
played 15 Pulled Fangs on a vampire under the original agrro rules, all it
meant was that he was sent to torpor 15 times. If you played one Pulled Fangs
on a vampire on its way to torpor, all that happened was that the vampire was
going to torpor a second time, and with no fangs. You could not burn a vampire
with Pulled Fangs when it was designed.

Right. Then, when they reprinted Jyhad as VTES, they changed the aggro rules,
and as such, Pulled Fangs (along with Ivory Bow and Wolf Claws type cards)
became *far* more powerful than originally intended. I strongly suspect that
this was not intentional--i.e. I do not belive that some game designer
somewhere said "Hmm. How do we make PF and Ivory Bow more powerful? I
know--we'll change the aggro rules!". If the effect that changing the aggro
rules had on PF was considered at all, I suspect it was an afterthought. With
the old Jyhad aggro rules, PF was allready verging on overpowered, as it had an
extremely powerful ability with negligible costs. Once it became possible to
burn a vampire with it, it became absurdly overpowered.

Check. Then, the rules team decided to fix the aggro rules to the current
version. As, under these aggro rules, PF could still burn vampires, it was
necessary to errata to maintain game balance, as that was the whole point of
the various rules changes and errata--to fix various aspects of the game that
were "wrong". PF was a pretty severe example of a card that was wrong.

Why was it wrong? Asside from the cost/effect imbalance, it allowed a Potence
combat deck to burn vampires left and right for negligible cost. Please compare
PF to Amaranth, assuming a Potence combat deck. PF simply burned a vampire
going to Torpor for no cost. Amaranth diablerized a vampire going to torpor,
which meant, in all likelyhood, the vampire playing the Amaranth was going to
be Blood Hunted out of existance. Poof. Why ever play Amaranth, when you have
Pulled Fangs to use? Oh, wait. There is no reason. Pulled Fangs was, when it
burned vampires every time it was played, simply too powerful.

Then, both Decapitiate and Disarm were designed and printed, as an example of
what the game designers (who apparently put down the crack pipe) considered
balanced cards, when compared to the abomination of Pulled Fangs. Disarm is an
incredibly similar card--play when you do more damage, has a lasting effect (no
limbs as opposed to no teeth), and has the exact same effect that PF did when
it was originally printed--it simply sent a vampire to torpor. The differences?
It requires a Discipline (a significant cost), and under the aggro rules that
were valid at the time, it was completele incapable of burning a vampire, as
was the intention of the original PF. Ok. Decapitate. It has the exact same
effect as PF did when it burned folks--it burns a vampire on the way to torpor,
just like PF did. Now, compare the costs. PF? Costs nothing. Decapitate?
Requires a superior Discipline and 2 blood-a significant cost. Apparently the
game designers came back to earth and said "Hey. It should be difficult to burn
vampires. PF simply was too powerful. Lets make a card that does the same
thing, but requires POT and a cost of 2 blood. That's balanced.", and so they
did.

Does it matter that Rush decks need to be able to reliably get rid of vampires?
No. Pulled Fangs was just too good. In any situation. Too powerful, not enough
of a cost. Thus, it was changed.

Raille wrote:
> Ask the right questions and finally get answers that give me enough
> detail to place just when the Pulled fangs are allowed to be played.
>
> Thank you LSJ!
>
> Anyhow for those following this thread here is a rather detailed
> breakdown of the damage resolution phase broken into its various parts
> and numbered. Excessively. Hey what can I say, I play Advanced Squad
> Leader and you just get used to these things. :)
>
> 6.4.6 Damage Resolution.
>
> 6.4.6.1 Damage resolution has three steps: damage calculation, prevent
> damage and heal damage.
>
> 6.4.6.2 Damage calculation.
>
> 6.4.6.2.1 Total all normal (ei non-agravated damage) from all sources.
> Damage that was made at the inapropriate range is reduced to zero, and
> is considered a null strike.
>
> 6.4.6.2.2 Total all agravated damage from all sources. Damage that was
> made at the inapropriate range is reduced to zero, and is considered a
> null strike.

Not quite. A strike/effect that is ineffective at the current range
has no effect. No damage is done, so none is reduced.

> 6.4.6.3 Apply total normal and agravated damage to the minion.

Damage calculation is done before damage resolution begins.
It is normally done in a "resolve strike" step (which first
applies damage to a minion and then resolves that damage).

X.X.X Play/produce some damage-dealing effect (amount of damage is
calculated at this time).
X.X.X.1 Apply damage (all damage from other, simultaneous, effects
is applied here before moving to the next step).
X.X.X.2 Resolve Damage (see 6.4.6)

6.4.6 Damage Resolution.

6.4.6.1 Prevent Damage

6.4.6.1.1 The minion taking damage can play damage prevention cards if
he is able to do so. These damage prevention cards are played one at a
time until all damage is prevented or the minion chooses not to play any
further cards.

> 6.4.6.4.1.1 Direct Intervention may be used at this point to prevent a
> damage prevention card from taking effect.

Shouldn't mention Direct Intervention here unless you mention it wherever
(minion) cards are played.

6.4.6.1.2 Damage prevention cards may be selectively used to prevent
aggravated damage before non-aggravated damage.

> 6.4.6.4.3 Only Minions can prevent damage.
>
> 6.4.6.4.4 Damage to retainers cannot be prevented.

These are the same rule.

6.4.6.1.3 Only Minions can prevent damage. Damage to retainers cannot
be prevented.

> 6.4.6.5 Any remaining damage (damage that was not prevented) is
> successfully inflicted. The damage is then healed, if the minion is a
> vampire, or causes a loss of life points if the minion is an ally or
> retainer.

(or, if aggravated, cannot be healed by a vampire and requires a wounded
vampire to burn blood to prevent destruction)

6.4.6.2 Any remaining damage (damage that was not prevented) is
successfully inflicted. The damage is then healed, if the minion is a
vampire, or causes a loss of life points if the minion is an ally or
retainer. If the damage is aggravated, it cannot be healed by a vampire
and requires a wounded vampire to burn blood to prevent destruction.
See 6.4.6.3.

> 6.4.6.5.1 Pulled fangs or disarm may be played at this time.

Not typically. It can only be played at this point if this point is
occuring during the press step. Otherwise, it'll have to wait until
the opposing vampire is "on his way to torpor" (or until the press
step is reached).

6.4.6.3 Healing damage.

> 6.4.6.6.1 Total all damage normal and agravated, that was not prevented
> in step
> (6.4.6.4) Prevent Damage.

The damage has already been totalled

> 6.4.6.6.2 For each point of damage inflicted on a vampire, burn one
> blood to heal that damage, starting with normal damage, then finishing
> with agravated damage.

Aggravated damage cannot be healed.

6.4.6.3.1. For each point of non-aggravated damage inflicted on a vampire,
burn one blood to heal that damage.

> 6.4.6.6.3 A vampire may burn ALL of his blood if needed, and doing so
> does not have any other negative effects on the vampire.

Recording every "no effect" avenue would be prohibitive - not sure if
this needs to be here.

> 6.4.6.6.4 If a vampire cannot heal all the damage, having taken more
> damge than there was blood to heal, blood is burned to heal what damage
> can be healed.

6.4.6.3.1.1 A vampire may burn ALL of his blood to heal if needed, and
doing so does not have any other negative effects on the vampire.

6.4.6.3.1.2 If a vampire cannot heal all the damage, having taken more
damge than there was blood to heal, blood is burned to heal what damage
can be healed. The rest is unhealed. (Unhealed damage causes a vampire
to go to torpor after damage resolution.)

> 6.4.6.6.5 Agravated damage is damage that a vampire cannot heal, like
> damage from sunlight or from claws or fangs of some other immortals,
> including vampires.
>
> 6.4.6.6.5.1 Since agravated damage cannot be healed, this send a vampire
> to torpor. Should there be unresolved agravated damage from step
> 6.4.6.6.4 the vampire is burned.

This doesn't allow for a single point of aggravated damage to burn a
wounded vampire (which it can).

6.4.6.3.2 Aggravated damage is damage that a vampire cannot heal.

6.4.6.3.2.1 Since it cannot be healed, aggravated damage causes a vampire
to go to torpor after damage resolution.

6.4.6.3.2.2 Aggravated damage done to a wounded vampire can burn the
vampire outright.

6.4.6.3.2.2.1 For each point of aggravated damage successfully inflicted on
a vampire who already has unhealed damage, he must burn a blood to prevent
his destruction.

6.4.6.3.2.2.2 If he doesn't have enough blood, he is burned.

> 6.4.6.6.5.2 A Vampire burned via unresolved agravated damage is not
> considered to have been diablerized and a blood hunt (6.5.6) cannot be
> called.

6.4.5.3.2.2.3 A vampire burned by aggravated damage is not considered to
have been diablerized and a blood hunt (6.5.6) cannot be called.

> 6.4.6.6.6 A vampire that has taken any agravated damage or normal damage
> in excess of its blood supply, goes to torpor.

This should be moved to after the "allies/retainer damage handling", for
coherence.

6.4.6.3.4 A vampire that has taken any damage that he has not healed goes
to torpor.

> 6.4.6.6.6.1 Cards effecting a vampire going to torpor can now be
> played.

That should be left up the the "card text" and not a rule proper, but OK.

6.4.6.3.4.1 Card affecting a vampire going to torpor can now be played.

And, if that is included, other similar sections should also be included:

6.4.6.3.2.2.2.1 Cards that are playable when a vampire/minion is burned
can now be played.

I would actually move both of these out of the "heal damage" rules and put
them in a "un-Ready a minion" effect. ("Whenever a minion is unReadied in
combat, move to the wrap-up-combat step")

> 6.4.6.6.6.2 Cards Such as taste of Vitae can now be played.

Taste of Vitae can only be played after strike resolution - not after
generic damage resolution. (Between 6.4.3.2 and whatever comes next:
6.4.3.3, 6.4.4, or "End of Round" (V.E of outline) if a combatant
has been unreadied.)

> 6.4.6.6.7 Each point of damage inflicted on a ally or retainer, from
> any source, agravated and non-agravated, causes the ally or retainer to
> lose one life counter.

6.4.6.3.3 Each point of damage, aggravated or non-aggravated, inflicted on
an ally or retainer causes the ally or retainer to lose one life counter.

> 6.4.6.6.7.1 An ally or retainer who loses all their life counters is
> burned.

6.4.6.3.3.1 An ally or retainer who loses all of his life counters is burned.

> Great a rules section I can come to grips with! YES!
>
> If LSJ would correct any reference to PFs above, such as moving the
> section from where it currently is, or adding additional references,
> please do so.

PF can be played at the end of a round. That is: during 6.4.4 (after
both minions have decided not to play any further presses), or, if the
round ends prematurely (due to a minion becoming unready, for instance),
during the "unReady a minion" step.

Probably there should be a step after 6.4.4 (like step V.E. of the
outline) in which the end-of-round effects (like PF) can be played.

> Still with pulled fangs, (and you thought I'd get away from that!) you
> generate a infinate loop. A easy manner to gain 1 VP in any game is to
> put 60 PFs in a deck, then play them all in the first combat where you
> inflict more damage that the other guy. Any +1 HD vampire will do.

That won't get you a VP - you still need to successfully withdraw (which
can't even begin until your next untap phase, after which you'd have to
avoid losing blood and losing pool and combat until your next untap phase.

Even so, how would that be different than just putting 60 Nosferatu
Putrescences in your 60 card deck and filling your crypt with Koko (and
playing all 60 NPs on Koko the first time she gets into combat)?

> Now that PFs has a place in the combat effects, why not just state the
> during section 6.4.6.6.8 you play PFs rather than 6.4.6.5.1. There is
> nothing in the rules that says exactly where the card goes.

See above. It goes after all strikes have been resolved (or all of them
that can be resolved), by necessity of the "inflicts more damage"
requirement. This has been ruled to be "at the end of the round" (without
regard to how the round is ending).

> Define the rules and some of these problems will go away by themselves.
> With PFs at the end of the cycle (such as 6.4.6.6.8) allows all previous
> damage to be resolved to its logical conclusion.

Yes, and then (at the end of the round, when the vampire may even still
be "on his way to torpor") another PF could be played. This is reinforced
by examining the fact that Amaranth could be played.

> Ok I lost you there didn't I. Logical in the game terms. Since a
> minion with two agro strikes only get the first because the change to a
> torpor status is SO FAST, that the blinding strike which mere mortals
> can't even see, failed to land it blow on the departing vampire.
>
> Another option is to have the Pulled fangs be played prior to the damage
> prevention phase. This might be more inline with the official rules,
> but causes a few head aches of its own. Minor one, but still, what
> would happen if Strike hands for 2, play 6 PFs during a dawn operation,
> then the other vampire plays skin of steel, nullifing both the strike
> and the host of PFs played.
>
> Actually I kind of like that. Leave the PFs without errata but make
> them usable prior to damage prevention. That allows vampires and minion
> in general to take the sting out of a PF deck.

Well - you couldn't play PF until you've discovered how much damage
both minions have inflicted (not just in the current strike, but in
the round as a whole). So that option is not workable.
